preschool.lesson: A leveraged AI-focused hedge fund nearly blew up.
paragraphs: Imagine a little money story called “The Investor Who Lost Big and Got More Famous.”

elementary.title: The Hedge Fund That Almost Blew Up and Became More Interesting
elementary.lesson: A leveraged AI-focused hedge fund nearly blew up. Wall Street saw a risk-management failure; Silicon Valley saw someone who might still be directionally right about a transformative technology.
paragraphs: Leopold Aschenbrenner is extremely excited about AI. He started a hedge fund called Situational Awareness and made lots of investments based on one big idea: AI is going to become incredibly important.
The fund bought companies AI might help and bet against companies AI might hurt. It looked like many bets. Then many started losing at once.
Imagine packing four pairs of shorts, two swimsuits and six pairs of sunglasses. You packed many things, but really you made one bet: it will be hot.
Situational Awareness had done something similar with AI, and it had borrowed money to make the bets bigger. When the trades went wrong, it lost a huge amount and had to sell investments.
On Wall Street, nearly blowing up your hedge fund is evidence something went wrong. In Silicon Valley, there is another possible reaction: Wow. This guy REALLY believes in AI.
Wall Street asks, “How much did you lose?” Silicon Valley sometimes asks, “Yes, but how enormous was the dream?”

middle.title: The Investor Who Lost Big and Got More Famous
middle.lesson: A leveraged AI-focused hedge fund nearly blew up. Wall Street saw a risk-management failure; Silicon Valley saw someone who might still be directionally right about a transformative technology.
paragraphs: A leveraged AI-focused hedge fund nearly blew up. Wall Street saw a risk-management failure; Silicon Valley saw someone who might still be directionally right about a transformative technology.

The financial mechanism matters because incentives change behavior. If a trade is cheap, easy or highly profitable for an intermediary, people will often do more of it. If a risk can be transferred, someone else has to be willing to hold it.
That creates second-order effects: prices can move before events happen, products built for institutions can spread to retail investors, and a hedge can quietly turn into a new concentrated bet.
The story is useful because it is not just about one company. It is a small example of how markets turn beliefs, risks and information into prices.

high.title: The Investor Who Lost Big and Got More Famous
high.lesson: A leveraged AI-focused hedge fund nearly blew up. Wall Street saw a risk-management failure; Silicon Valley saw someone who might still be directionally right about a transformative technology.
paragraphs: A leveraged AI-focused hedge fund nearly blew up. Wall Street saw a risk-management failure; Silicon Valley saw someone who might still be directionally right about a transformative technology.

The important analytical move is to separate the economic exposure from the legal or marketing label. A product called a hedge may still contain concentrated factor risk; a security device is only as strong as its key generation; a market structure can redistribute costs between retail traders, institutions and intermediaries.

Then look at incentives. Who earns a spread, fee or markup? Who benefits from more volume? Who is paid for taking tail risk? Who gets information first? Those questions usually explain why the arrangement exists.

Finally, ask what would make the story reverse. Markets price expectations, so the surprise is often not the event itself but the difference between what happened and what everyone had already prepared for.

preschool.title: The Price That Kept Running
preschool.lesson: Momentum means buying things that are already rising because you think they will keep rising.
paragraphs: Imagine a little money story called “The Price That Kept Running.”
Someone has a problem. Money can help move the problem around, but it cannot make every problem disappear.

That is the big idea in this story.

elementary.title: The Trade That Says 'It Is Going Up, So Buy It'
elementary.lesson: Momentum means buying things that are already rising because you think they will keep rising. Intraday versions try to capture short trends within a single trading day, especially on volatile days.
paragraphs: There are complicated ways to choose investments. Momentum has a wonderfully simple summary: this thing is going up, so maybe it will keep going up.
Intraday momentum tries to catch that movement inside one trading day. A computer spots something running upward, buys it, and hopes to get out before the running stops.
This sounds a bit like chasing someone because they are already running.
Which it is.
But if prices do it often enough, people will build extremely serious mathematical systems for doing the chasing.

preschool.title: The Tiny Step That Wasn't So Tiny
preschool.lesson: Prediction contracts often trade between $0 and $1.
paragraphs: Imagine a little money story called “The Tiny Step That Wasn't So Tiny.”
Someone has a problem. Money can help move the problem around, but it cannot make every problem disappear.
The trick is to ask: Who gets the good surprise? Who gets the bad surprise? And who gets paid for taking the chance?

elementary.title: How Finance Made Everyone Care About One Penny
elementary.lesson: Prediction contracts often trade between $0 and $1. A one-cent minimum price move can therefore be a large percentage spread, which can make frequent retail trading lucrative for market makers but expensive for large hedgers.
paragraphs: Prediction-market contracts often cost less than one dollar, so a penny can be a surprisingly big deal.
If a contract costs 10 cents, paying 11 cents is about 10% more. For a $200 stock, a one-cent difference is almost nothing.
Markets have a smallest allowed price step, called a tick. On many prediction contracts it is one cent.
That can be good for traders who stand between buyers and sellers and earn the difference.
A penny is normally the coin you ignore on the sidewalk. Finance has found a way to make extremely serious adults care deeply about it.

preschool.lesson: Private equity often means highly trained financiers buying and improving ordinary businesses such as pest-control companies.

elementary.title: Private Equity's Extremely Glamorous Pest-Control Era
elementary.lesson: Private equity often means highly trained financiers buying and improving ordinary businesses such as pest-control companies. The article jokes about private-equity professionals suddenly being treated as glamorous celebrity partners.
paragraphs: Private-equity firms buy companies, try to improve them and later sell them. The companies do not have to be glamorous.
They might make industrial parts, run dental offices or kill bugs. A useful pest-control business can make perfectly good money even if nobody makes a movie about it.
Private-equity people themselves, however, have somehow become glamorous in certain corners of culture. Articles discuss them as desirable boyfriends. Celebrities date financiers.
So there is a pleasing mismatch.
By day: an extremely serious meeting about the profit margins of regional pest-control companies.
By night: apparently, heartthrob.
